rows.title: Parallel evaluation of ASP programs:techniques and implementation
rows.summary:
Answer Set Programming (ASP) is a purely declarative programming paradigm
based on nonmonotonic reasoning and logic programming. The idea of ASP
is to represent a given computational problem by a logic program such that
its answer sets correspond to solutions, and then, use an answer set solver
to find such solutions. The ASP language is very expressive and allows the
representation of high-complexity problems (i.e., every problem in the second
level of the polynomial hierarchy); unfortunately, the expressive power of the
language comes at the price of an elevated cost of answer set computation. Even
if this fact has initially discouraged the development of ASP system, nowadays
several implementations are available, and the interest for ASP is growing in
the scientific community as well as in the field of industry.
In the last few years, significant technological enhancements have been achie-
ved in the design of computer architectures, with a move towards the adoption
of multi-core microprocessors. As a consequence, Symmetric Multi-Processing
(SMP) has become available even on non-dedicated machines. Indeed, at the

rows.title: New Lower Bounds for Some Multicolored Ramsey Numbers
rows.summary: In this article we use two different methods to find new lower bounds for some multicolored Ramsey numbers. In the first part we use the finite field method used by Greenwood and Gleason [GG] to show that $R(5,5,5) \geq 242$ and $R(6,6,6) \geq 692$. In the second part we extend Fan Chung's result in [C] to show that, $$ R(3,3,3,k_1,k_2,\dots,k_r) \geq 3 R(3,3,k_1,k_2,\dots,k_r) + R(k_1,k_2,\dots,k_r) - 3 $$ holds for any natural number $r$ and for any $k_i\geq 3$, $i=1,2,\dots r$. This general result, along with known results, imply the following nontrivial bounds: $R(3,3,3,4) \geq 91$, $R(3,3,3,5) \geq 137$, $R(3,3,3,6) \geq 165$, $R(3,3,3,7) \geq 220$, $R(3,3,3,9) \geq 336$, and $R(3,3,3,11) \geq 422$.

rows.title: Generalized Ramsey Theory for Graphs. II. Small Diagonal Numbers
rows.summary: Consider a finite nonnull graph G with no loops or multiple edges and no isolated points. Its Ramsey number r ( G ) r(G) is defined as the minimum number p such that every 2-coloring of the lines of the complete graph K p {K_p} must contain a monochromatic G . This generalizes the classical diagonal Ramsey numbers r ( n , n ) = r ( K n ) r(n,n) = r({K_n}) . We obtain the exact value of the Ramsey number of every such graph with at most four points.

rows.title: Combinatorial Relations and Chromatic Graphs
rows.summary: Greenwood, R. E.; Gleason, A. M. Canadian Journal of Mathematics 7 (1955), 1-7. The classical paper establishing small Ramsey numbers by explicit constructions and chromatic-graph arguments: it proves R(3,3)=6 and R(3,4)=9 (i.e. every red/blue colouring of the edges of K_9 contains a red triangle or a blue K_4, while K_8 admits a colouring avoiding both), and gives the corresponding partition relations. This is the standard origin cited for R(3,4)=9. Retrieved via Crossref (DOI verified against the Canadian Journal of Mathematics record). Note: full text is not on the local shelf (crossref record has no pdf_url), so this row is metadata-only until a fulltext is fetched.

rows.title: Small Ramsey Numbers
rows.summary: Radziszowski, Stanisław. "Small Ramsey Numbers", The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, Dynamic Survey DS1 (DOI 10.37236/21). The standard continuously maintained survey/table of known small Ramsey numbers; its tables list the classical values including R(3,4)=9 (attributed to Greenwood-Gleason 1955), together with the known bounds for neighbouring cases and the references for each entry. Retrieved via Crossref (DOI verified against the EJC record); this is the survey of record for citing the value R(3,4)=9.
